name: Grok face rating

lead: Grok face rating means giving Grok, the chatbot from xAI built into X, a selfie and asking it to score attractiveness, usually out of 10, or to comment on symmetry, proportions and features. People use it as a fast, free second opinion on their face and as a way to track changes after a new haircut, grooming routine or weight change.

Grok's behaviour is inconsistent: users have posted refusals, middling scores and very high scores. A September 2026 preprint comparing four chatbots with human raters on 102 face photos found Grok gave the highest average ratings and agreed least with humans.

paras: Users post or upload a photo, often on X by tagging Grok, and ask for a rating on a 1-10 or 1-100 scale or for a breakdown by feature (jaw, eyes, skin, symmetry). Some compare results across angles, lighting or before and after photos, or ask what to change. Scores are treated as informal feedback and are commonly repeated with different prompts.

Responses vary run to run and with the prompt, and the preprint found Grok's scores diverged from human averages. Uploading a face photo shares biometric-type data with a platform. Commentators have argued such ratings reinforce narrow beauty standards, and Grok itself has at times replied that it does not rank attractiveness.

angle.text: People use Grok as an always-available outside opinion on their face and as a way to compare changes such as a new haircut, beard or weight loss. The feedback is machine-generated and varies between runs, so users often repeat prompts and compare.

lead: Grok face rating is a looksmaxxing-adjacent practice in which users ask xAI's Grok chatbot to score or critique the attractiveness of a face photo. Grok received image understanding in October 2024 and is integrated into X, which let users tag it under a selfie [1].

Responses vary. Posts on X show Grok declining, saying it does not rank attractiveness, and also giving numeric scores or feature-by-feature breakdowns. Users treat the outputs as a quick, private benchmark for experiments with hair, grooming, facial hair or photography.

A preprint covered by PsyPost in September 2026 compared GPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok with ratings from 2,513 humans on 102 face photos. Grok gave the highest average rating (5.21 on a 1-7 scale versus 3.02 for humans) and agreed least with the human raters [2].
infobox: 2026 preprint comparing four AI models with human raters

paras: Users upload a face photo to Grok or reply to their own post tagging it, and request a rating, often 1-10, or an analysis of symmetry, proportions and features measured against what it calls conventional standards. Output ranges from a short refusal to a structured breakdown.

On X, Grok has said it cannot rank attractiveness, citing a focus on avoiding objectification and biased beauty standards. Other users have posted numeric scores, including low and very high ones, and one user reported a refusal followed by an offer to generate a stylised image instead. Results depend on the prompt, photo and model version.

The preprint by Grandas and colleagues used the 102-photo Face Research Lab London Set and prior ratings from 2,513 people. All four chatbots rated faces higher than humans, with AI mean 4.71 versus 3.02. Grok averaged 5.21, was the only model to give any face the top score, and agreed least with humans and other models [2]. Some online commentators have argued that chatbot beauty scoring can reinforce rigid standards, particularly for women.

The practice sits alongside face-rating apps, PSL ratings and community rate threads, offering a quick automated option. Users often combine it with photo experiments, such as comparing angles and lighting, since the score can shift with the image.
No studies found. The 2026 preprint above is a non-peer-reviewed comparison of AI and human ratings, not a clinical study [2].
